insider_note: Whenever the argument of a square root is linear in x, the setter usually picks limits so both endpoints give perfect squares — a signal the answer will be a clean integer.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Integrate using the linear substitution rule
steps.margin_note: First mark. The antiderivative of 1/√(ax+b) is (1/a)·2√(ax+b) — here a=2.
steps.memory_tip: ∫dx/√(ax+b) = (2/a)√(ax+b) + c — a fixed pattern for any linear expression inside a square root.
steps.why: For √(ax+b), the antiderivative is (1/a)·2√(ax+b) because differentiating √(ax+b) gives a/(2√(ax+b)); the extra factor 1/a compensates for the constant 2 sitting inside the square root.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the factor 1/2 that comes from the linear substitution 2x−1.
Writing the antiderivative as √(2x−1)/2 instead of √(2x−1).

steps.label: Apply the limits
steps.margin_note: Second mark. √9 = 3 and √1 = 1 — both perfect squares, so the answer is a whole number.
steps.memory_tip: Always substitute the UPPER limit first, then subtract the value at the LOWER limit.
steps.why: Substituting the upper limit 5 and the lower limit 1 into √(2x−1) gives √9 and √1, and subtracting the lower value from the upper value gives the final result.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the limits in the wrong order.
